sentences.text: Atychodracon was a medium-sized carnivorous plesiosaur reaching lengths of 5 to 5.29 meters.
Among early plesiosaurs, this animal possessed a relatively large skull that accounted for 16% of its total body length.
The snout featured a premaxillary section where the width and length were roughly equal, containing five teeth.
Based on the holotype, the skeleton included 29 to 30 neck vertebrae and approximately 32 tail vertebrae.
The forelimb bones show a robust humerus and an inverse relationship between the radius length and the ulna length.
The lower jaw symphysis was expanded to the sides, with its width nearly matching its length.
The species name megacephalus translates to "large-headed," highlighting the skull's massive size relative to the rest of the skeleton.
Despite the destruction of the original specimen, the genus is relatively well-represented by a neotype and two additional individuals.
The genus Atychodracon was formally established by Smith in 2015.
The only known species, Atychodracon megacephalus, was originally named in 1846 by Samuel Stutchbury as a species of Plesiosaurus.
The original holotype specimen was destroyed in a World War II air raid in 1940, leading to the designation of a neotype.
Recent studies indicate little close relationship between Atychodracon and true Rhomaleosaurus species, sharing only general rhomaleosaurid traits.
Cladistic analyses found "R." megacephalus to be basal to the clade containing Rhomaleosaurus and Eurycleidus, supporting its placement in its own genus.
Among other romaleosaurids, Atychodracon material has been referred mainly to two genera before its separation, namely Rhomaleosaurus and Eurycleidus.
Atychodracon belongs to the family Rhomaleosauridae.
The holotype dates to the earliest Hettangian stage, approximately 201 million years ago.
Atychodracon is an extinct genus of rhomaleosaurid plesiosaur known from the Late Triassic–Early Jurassic boundary of England.
The Blue Lias, also known as the Lower Lias, dates to the Upper Triassic-Lower Jurassic boundary, including the Rhaetian, Hettangian, and lower Sinemurian stages.
However, it is possible that some specimens from the area originate from slightly younger deposits.
It is debated whether Atychodracon is closely related to Eurycleidus, as some analyses support a sister-taxon relationship while others do not.
